title: He who is (ST I.13.11)
hookLine: the best name for God is he who is, being itself

lines: A BUSH THAT ISN'T BURNED UP.
A NAME THAT'S BARELY A NAME.
cards: A shepherd stands barefoot on a mountainside in front of a bush that burns and is not burned up. A voice has just told him to go back to Egypt and bring his people out. Moses has a practical worry.
When I tell them the God of their fathers sent me, they'll ask his name. What do I say? The answer is a name that's barely a name at all.
You first stood at this bush on day two hundred ninety-five. Now Thomas Aquinas asks which name for God fits best. Today's word is that name.

teach.b: Here is God's answer to Moses, in the Douay-Rheims: "I AM WHO AM." And then: "Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you." Thomas asks whether He who is is the most fitting name for God.
Yes, he says, for three reasons. First, what it means.

teach.h: NOT A KIND OF THING: TO BE.
teach.b: Every other name names a kind of thing, or a quality. Rock. Shepherd.
Wise. Good. This one names no kind at all.
It names to be. And two days ago, Thomas said that in God, what God is and that God is are one. So a name that means simply is fits as no other does.
Second, how open it is. Other names narrow God to one side; this one sets no edge.
Thomas quotes an earlier teacher, John Damascene: this name holds being itself like a sea without limit or bound. Remember the girl who couldn't see the other side. Third, the tense.
Not he who was. Not he who will be. He who is.
Following Augustine, Thomas says there is no past or future in God.

teach.h: HE WHO IS, HATH SENT ME TO YOU.
teach.b: Then, careful as ever, a turn. In another respect, he says, the name God, and the holy name written in the Hebrew Bible, are more proper still, because they name God alone.

No single name holds God; each catches something. That's analogy, carried all the way. But Thomas keeps a special place for this one: the name that points not at something God has, but at what God is.

how: Catholic theology, following Thomas, often speaks of God as being itself, and Catholics hear the name from the burning bush in the readings at Mass when Exodus 3 is read.

o: a title for Moses as God's chosen messenger
God's name to Moses: being itself, always now
the name of the angel seen in the burning bush

games.q: he who is — tap the pairs.
p: no past or future in God

s: Thomas says 'He who is' names one kind of thing among others
he says it names no kind at all: it names to be itself.
Thomas takes the name from Exodus, where Moses asks God's name
God answers, I AM WHO AM, and tells Moses to say HE WHO IS sent him.
Thomas says no name for God is more proper in any respect
he adds that in another respect the name God, and the holy name of the Hebrew Bible, are more proper still.

games.q: you're Moses at the burning bush. you ask: if they want to know your name, what do I tell them? what does God answer?
o: the God of this mountain sent you.
tell them no name at all.
games.why: "I AM WHO AM ... HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you." Thomas calls this the most fitting name for God: being itself, without limit, always now.

practice: If you pray, say two words slowly under your breath, God is, adding nothing, let them go quiet, then say them again on the next breath. If you don't pray, try the smallest word of all, is: the floor is, the breath is, the room is.
Either way you're not describing anything, only standing before being, the way Moses stood before the bush.

wordCard.voice: He who is. The name God gives Moses in Exodus, which Thomas Aquinas calls the most fitting name for God: not a kind of thing, but being itself, always now.

orig.note: Latin, from the Vulgate of Exodus 3:14: he who is — the name Thomas calls most proper to God.

carryVoice: Your line: being itself. A name with no edge and no past. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.q: Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you.

sources.ref: Summa Theologiae I, q. 13, a. 11 (body and reply to objection 1)
